entry.title: A Step-by-Step Guide to Data Product Activation in SAP Business Data Cloud
entry.content:
Enterprise data is rarely contained within a single system. Organizations rely on data distributed across multiple applications to support reporting, analytics, AI initiatives, and operational decision-making. Making this data available across platforms while maintaining business context, governance, and consistency remains a significant challenge.

SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) is SAP's modern data platform that brings data from different SAP systems into one secure and organized environment. It helps businesses manage, govern, and analyze data more efficiently while supporting analytics and AI-driven insights.

One of the key features of BDC is Data Products. Data Products are predefined, business-contextualized datasets designed to provide reusable, governed, and semantically enriched enterprise data assets. Instead of repeatedly extracting data and rebuilding its business context for individual use cases, organizations can use Data Products to make trusted enterprise data available for downstream consumption.

Related Data Products are grouped under a Parent Package, which acts as a collection for a specific business area. This makes it easier for organizations to activate and manage complete business domains in a consistent and scalable way.

In this walkthrough, we explore the complete Data Product activation lifecycle in SAP Business Data Cloud, from discovery and prerequisite validation to activation, monitoring, and sharing with SAP Databricks and SAP Datasphere.

 

Exploring Data Products in SAP Business Accelerator Hub

The SAP Business Accelerator Hub provides a central location for exploring available Data Products and business content packages.

Users can browse datasets across different business domains, review available capabilities, and understand relevant dependencies before beginning the activation process within SAP Business Data Cloud.

Start by accessing the available Data Products through the SAP Business Accelerator Hub. Select the Data Product you want to activate and review its associated business content and capabilities.

Data Product URL: https://api.sap.com/dataproducts

Data Products are organized into Parent Packages, which group related business entities and datasets within a common business context. Selecting a Parent Package provides visibility into the associated Data Products available for activation.

Explore the Data Products available within the Parent Package to identify the datasets relevant to the business requirement.

Prerequisites: Reviewing the Required SAP Notes

Before installing or activating a Data Product, the source environment must meet the required technical prerequisites.

The relevant SAP Notes and package-specific dependencies should be reviewed and implemented before proceeding with the activation process.

Before proceeding with Data Product installation, validate that all applicable prerequisites have been successfully implemented and are in complete status in transaction SNOTE.

Identifying dependencies, authorization requirements, and release compatibility before installation provides a stronger foundation for the subsequent activation steps.

From our experience, Data Product activation should not begin with installation. Reviewing dependencies, authorization requirements, and release compatibility upfront is an important part of preparing the environment for the activation process.

 

Data Product Activation: Step-by-Step Process

Step 1: Access the SAP Business Data Cloud Cockpit

Once the prerequisites have been addressed, log in to SAP Business Data Cloud and access the BDC Cockpit.

The Cockpit serves as the central workspace for managing Data Products, configuring system connections, monitoring activities, and administering the platform. 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Cockpit Section

Description

Home Overview

Dashboard for system status, activities, and recent updates. Use this as your starting point.

Intelligent Apps & Data Packages

Pre-built apps and data models designed for specific business use cases.

Catalog & Marketplace

Central repository to search, browse, and access available data assets and products.

System Landscape

Manage connected systems, users, integration settings, and configurations.

Monitoring

Track system health, data pipeline flows, connectivity status, and error logs.

Step 2: Configure the System Landscape

Before installing a Data Package, the required source and target system connections must be configured.

Navigate to the System Landscape section of the BDC Cockpit and, with support from the platform administrator, establish the necessary connections.

This step creates the technical foundation for the subsequent activation and sharing processes.

Step 3: Install the Data Package

Once the system connections have been configured, navigate to Intelligent Apps & Data Packages.

Select the required Data Package containing the business-specific Data Products that you want to activate and begin the installation process.

After installation, verify that the package is available within the SAP Business Data Cloud environment.

Installing the package makes the relevant Data Products available within the environment. The required Data Products can then be selected and activated based on the business requirement.

One distinction that is important during the process is that Data Package installation and Data Product activation are separate stages. Installing the package makes the relevant Data Products available within the environment, while activation prepares the selected Data Products for downstream use.

Step 4: Activate the Required Data Products

After the Data Package has been successfully installed, select the Data Products required for the use case.

For this walkthrough, we use Data Products from the SAP Accounting and Financial Close domain, including Company and Company Code.

Depending on the business requirement, individual Data Products can be selected for activation, or multiple available Data Products within the package can be enabled.


Before starting activation, select the appropriate source system and run the system readiness pre-check.

 

.

Once the readiness checks have been completed, begin the activation process.

Step 5: Monitor and Validate the Activation

After activation begins, navigate to the Monitoring section of the BDC Cockpit to track progress and review operational status.

Navigate to Data Flow Monitoring and review the activated Data Products and their associated business objects.

For the Company Code Data Product, you can see associated objects such as:

  • Currency Role of Company CodeCurrency Role of Company Code
  • Currency TranslationCurrency Translation
  • Company Code HierarchyCompany Code Hierarchy
  • Company Code Hierarchy NodeCompany Code Hierarchy Node
  • Company Code Hierarchy Node - TextCompany Code Hierarchy Node - Text
  • Company Code Hierarchy - TextCompany Code Hierarchy - Text
  • Currency RoleCurrency Role
  • Currency Role - TextCurrency Role – Text

Similarly, validate the Company Data Product to confirm that its associated datasets and business relationships are available.

In our experience, successful activation should not be treated as the end of the workflow. Reviewing the associated business objects, relationships, and hierarchies in Data Flow Monitoring is an important validation step before making the Data Products available for downstream consumption.

Step 6: Access the Data Products in Catalog & Marketplace

Once the Data Products have been successfully activated and validated, navigate to Catalog & Marketplace.

Search for and select the required Data Product.

When the Data Product reaches Active status, it becomes available for sharing and consumption across supported platforms, including SAP Databricks, SAP Datasphere, and Enterprise Databricks.

Select the required Data Product and click Share to begin the sharing process.

Step 7: Share the Data Product with SAP Databricks

To make the activated Data Product available within SAP Databricks, select the Data Product, click Share, and choose Add Target.

Select the target system and specify the Share Name and SAP Databricks workspace.

Once configuration is complete, click Share.

After sharing is complete, log in to SAP Databricks and verify that the Data Product is available within the configured workspace.

Step 8: Deploy the Data Product to SAP Datasphere

Log in to SAP Datasphere and navigate to Catalog & Marketplace. Search for the activated Data Product, select it, and complete the installation process to make it available for consumption in Datasphere.

Then, specify the Target Space where the Data Product should be shared or deployed for consumption.

You have two options to proceed:

  • Replication Flow
  • Remote Table

Select the option that best fits your requirements, then click Start Import & Deploy to complete the setup in SAP Datasphere and make the Data Product available for use.

Check the deployment status in the Monitoring section and review the Task Logs in SAP Datasphere to confirm that the process has been completed successfully without errors.

After deployment is completed, go to the repository in SAP Datasphere and verify that all activated Data Products are available and successfully deployed.

Key Takeaways from the Data Product Activation Process

  • Activation begins before entering the BDC Cockpit. Reviewing SAP Notes, package dependencies, release compatibility, and authorization requirements is an important part of preparing the environment.
  • Data Package installation and Data Product activation are separate stages. 
  • Successful activation should be followed by monitoring and validation. 
  • Downstream consumption requirements should be considered as part of the overall architecture. 

Conclusion

SAP Business Data Cloud provides a structured approach to making governed, reusable, and business-ready enterprise data available across modern data and analytics platforms.

Through the Data Product activation lifecycle, organizations can discover relevant Data Products, prepare the technical environment, install and activate the required datasets, validate their availability, and make them accessible to downstream platforms.

Discover  →  Prepare  →  Connect  →  Install  →  Activate  →  Monitor  →  Validate  →  Share  →  Consume

By combining governed Data Products with platforms such as SAP Databricks and SAP Datasphere, organizations can establish a stronger foundation for enterprise reporting, analytics, AI, and data-driven decision-making.

entry.title: From SAP APIs to AI Tools: Building an AI-Ready SAP Integration Platform
entry.content:
Introduction

Artificial Intelligence is rapidly changing the way users interact with enterprise applications. Rather than navigating multiple interfaces or searching through complex systems, users increasingly expect to retrieve business information using natural language. For SAP landscapes, however, enabling this type of interaction presents a unique challenge.

SAP offers a rich ecosystem of APIs through the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, covering a wide range of business domains such as Finance, Procurement, Inventory Management, and Master Data. While these APIs provide extensive business capabilities, they are primarily designed for system-to-system integration. Their technical structure, OData entities, and complex payloads make them difficult to consume directly by AI assistants or business users.

Business users rarely think in terms of API names or technical endpoints. Instead, they think in terms of business tasks, such as:

  • What is the balance of G/L Account 400000?
  • Show the details of Cost Centre IT100.
  • List all open Purchase Orders.
  • How much stock is available for Material MAT100?

This highlights the need for an abstraction layer that translates business requests into SAP API calls while presenting the results in a simple and meaningful way.

To address this challenge, the project was developed in two stages. The first stage focused on designing and prototyping the business tools using SAP Business Application Studio (BAS), where each tool was implemented as a CAP service with mock business data. This phase allowed the business logic, service contracts, and response structures to be validated independently of external SAP systems.

The second stage focused on integrating real SAP business data by replacing the mock implementations with live APIs from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub. These tools were then exposed through a Remote MCP Server deployed on SAP BTP Kyma, allowing AI assistants such as Claude Desktop to invoke business-oriented tools instead of interacting directly with low-level SAP APIs.

Designing Business-Oriented AI Tools

Before implementing the technical solution, the first step was to identify common business scenarios that users perform within SAP systems. Instead of exposing individual SAP APIs directly, the objective was to design reusable AI tools that represent meaningful business actions.

The tools were organized into three functional domains:

  • Finance – General Ledger, Cost Centres, Profit Centres, Budget Validation, and Open Accounting Items.
  • Procurement – Purchase Orders, Goods Receipt/Invoice Receipt reconciliation, and Material Stock availability.
  • Master Data – Business Partner information for customers and suppliers.

Each tool encapsulates one or more SAP APIs behind a business-oriented operation, allowing AI assistants to interact with SAP using business terminology rather than technical API names.

 

Figure 1. Overall Architecture of the AI Business Tool Platform

Prototyping the AI Business Tools with SAP Business Application Studio

The initial implementation focused on validating the business tools before integrating with live SAP systems. SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) was used to prototype each tool as an independent SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) service.

Each tool was designed with two main components:

  • Service Definition (.cds) – Defines the service contract by specifying the service name, the business action exposed by the tool, the required input parameters, and the structure of the returned data. For example, a Cost Centre tool may accept a Cost Centre ID as input and return information such as the Cost Centre name, Company Code, responsible person, and status.
  • Service Implementation (.js) – Implements the business logic behind the service. It processes the input parameters, performs the required validations, retrieves or simulates the relevant business data, handles potential errors, and returns the response according to the structure defined in the CDS service.

During the prototyping phase, mock business data was used within the JavaScript implementation to simulate SAP responses. This approach enabled the service contracts, input validation, response structures, and business logic to be thoroughly tested without requiring connectivity to external SAP systems.

Once the prototypes were validated, the mock implementations could be seamlessly replaced with live SAP Business Accelerator Hub APIs while preserving the same business-oriented service interface.

CAP Service Structure

Component

Responsibility

CDS Layer (.cds)

Defines the service contract, including the exposed actions, input parameters, and response structure.

JavaScript Layer (.js)

Implements the business logic, processes requests, retrieves data, and returns the appropriate response.

 

Integrating SAP Business Accelerator Hub APIs

After validating the prototypes, the next step was to replace the mock business data with live SAP APIs available through the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

The SAP Business Accelerator Hub provides a comprehensive catalog of SAP APIs covering multiple business domains, including Finance, Procurement, Human Resources, Supply Chain, and Master Data. Each API includes detailed documentation, OData service definitions, request examples, and a sandbox environment for testing.

 

Figure 2. SAP Business Accelerator Hub provides a centralized catalog of SAP APIs, documentation, and sandbox environments for validating business scenarios.

Reference: SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

For this project, the Business Accelerator Hub served as the primary source for identifying, validating, and integrating the SAP APIs behind each AI business tool. Although multiple APIs were integrated throughout the project, the Business Partner API is used in this article as a representative example to illustrate the overall integration process.

 

Figure 3. Business Partner API overview showing the available operations, documentation, and sandbox support.

Reference. Overview | Business Partner (A2X) | SAP Business Accelerator Hub

The integration process consisted of four main activities:

  1. API Discovery

Identifying the SAP APIs that best matched each business scenario by exploring the SAP Business Accelerator Hub catalog.

  1. API Validation

Testing the selected APIs using the SAP Business Accelerator Hub Sandbox to understand the available entities, query parameters, supported operations, and response structures before implementation.

 

Figure 4. The SAP Business Accelerator Hub sandbox was used to validate API requests, parameters, and expected responses before integrating the APIs into the AI tools.

Reference. Try Out | Business Partner (A2X) | SAP Business Accelerator Hub

  1. Business Mapping

Mapping technical SAP APIs to business-oriented AI tools, ensuring that each tool represented a meaningful business operation rather than exposing technical endpoints directly.

  1. Response Simplification

Extracting only the business-relevant fields from the SAP responses to produce concise, AI-friendly outputs while maintaining a consistent response structure.

 

Figure 5. Sample response returned by the Business Partner API, demonstrating the business data consumed by the AI tools.

Building the Remote MCP Server on SAP BTP Kyma

After integrating the SAP Business Accelerator Hub APIs, the next step was to expose the business tools through a Remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.

The MCP server acts as an intermediary layer between AI assistants and SAP systems. Rather than allowing AI clients to invoke SAP APIs directly, the server exposes a collection of business-oriented tools that internally execute the required SAP API calls, process the responses, and return only the relevant business information.

For this project, the MCP server was deployed as a Node.js Function on SAP BTP Kyma Runtime, providing a lightweight and scalable environment for hosting AI-enabled services.

 

Figure 6. SAP BTP Kyma namespace hosting the Remote MCP Server and supporting Kubernetes resources.

The server implementation included the following components:

  • MCP Server Initialization – Configured the Remote MCP Server using the Model Context Protocol SDK.

 

Figure 7. Remote MCP Server deployed as a Node.js Function in SAP BTP Kyma.

  • Tool Registration – Registered each AI business tool together with its input schema and execution logic.

 

Figure 8. SAP BTP Kyma Function implementing the Remote MCP Server and registering the available AI tools.

  • Streamable HTTP Transport – Enabled communication between AI clients and the remote server using the MCP Streamable HTTP protocol.
  • SAP API Integration – Connected the registered tools to the corresponding SAP Business Accelerator Hub APIs.
  • Environment Configuration – Used Kubernetes Secrets and Environment Variables to securely provide API credentials to the application.

 

Figure 9. Kubernetes Secret storing the SAP API key securely outside the application source code.

This architecture allows AI assistants to invoke high-level business operations while the MCP server manages authentication, API communication, response transformation, and error handling behind the scenes.

Connecting the Remote MCP Server to Claude Desktop

With the Remote MCP Server deployed on SAP BTP Kyma, the final step was to make the business tools available to an AI assistant. For this project, Claude Desktop was used as the MCP client.

Claude Desktop supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and can connect to remote MCP servers through a Streamable HTTP endpoint. Once connected, Claude automatically discovers the tools exposed by the server together with their descriptions and input schemas.

The connection process involved three simple steps:

  1. Registering the Remote MCP Server by providing the server's Streamable HTTP endpoint.
  2. Granting tool permissions to allow Claude to invoke the available business tools.
  3. Verifying the connection, ensuring that Claude successfully discovered the exposed MCP tools.

Once the connection was established, the SAP business tools became available inside Claude Desktop as native AI tools. From that point onward, users could invoke business operations using natural language without interacting directly with SAP APIs or understanding their technical implementation.

 

Figure 10. Claude Desktop connected to the Remote MCP Server

This architecture demonstrates how SAP business capabilities can be securely exposed to AI assistants while keeping the integration logic centralized within the Remote MCP Server.

Conclusion

This project demonstrates how SAP Business Accelerator Hub APIs can be transformed into reusable AI business tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By combining SAP Business Application Studio for prototyping, SAP BTP Kyma for deployment, and Claude Desktop as the AI client, it is possible to expose SAP business capabilities through a secure, business-oriented interface.

Rather than interacting directly with technical APIs, AI assistants invoke high-level business operations while the MCP server manages authentication, API communication, and response transformation. This architecture provides a scalable foundation for integrating enterprise SAP systems with modern AI assistants and can be extended to additional SAP business domains.

entry.title: Is it Death of SAP FRICEW/RICEFW Gaps due to the Rise of Agents? Clean Core or AI Core?
entry.content:
*The views expressed here are solely my own and do not represent those of any entity or organization.*

How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Started Loving Autonomous ERP and Business AI Platform (BAIP)?

FRICEW/RICEFW - A Nostalgic Farewell to Chaos

Remember RICEFW? Reports. Interfaces. Conversions. Enhancements. Forms. Workflows For two decades, RICEFW was the SAP consultant's security blanket i.e. the comforting framework that explained away every business requirement that vanilla S/4HANA couldn't handle.

RICEFW wasn't a framework. It was a permission slip. It was the "just customize it" drug that kept enterprises strung out on technical debt. Every RICEFW artifact cost money to maintain. Every report and interface was a fragile bridge built on hope and handwritten code from ABAP developers who had long since left the organization. And every time SAP released an update, the basis team braced for impact.

Then Joule walked in.

When AI Met Your Messy Customizations and The Plot Twist Nobody Expected

It's 2026. SAP Joule and BAIP isn't a cute copilot anymore. It's an agentic AI platform. It thinks. It plans. It executes. It knows your business rules. Here's where it gets interesting:

Joule agents can do things RICEFW did. But better. Autonomously. Without breaking on every upgrade.

Let me give an example with a report and interface :

Imagine your Tuesday 3 AM report.

Old world involves writing ABAP code, manual scheduling, someone getting paged when it fails.

New world will describe the business logic in plain language (or use Joule Studio), an agent understands your data model, your authorization rules, and your governance boundaries and it can run dashboard in real-time.

That special XML interface that your special vendor needs? A Joule agent that understands your source systems, the vendor's requirements, and SAP's security model can orchestrate the extraction, transformation, and delivery. No code. No maintenance nightmares. Just business logic in motion.

We are not yet at RICEFW's death spiral, as widespread human adoption and AI maturity will take time. However, in the future, this could lead to a resurgence of data governance and security.

RICEFW Dead? - The Answer That Will Break Your Basis Team's Heart

Short Answer: No, RICEFW isn't dead; it's getting married. It's evolving into something that delivers business value without the technical burden, provided you accept that agents are always right and they behave.

Long Answer: It's complicated, but also quite elegant. It will require all non-SAP teams to communicate closely and work together effectively. Agent to Agent divorces are a bit more challenging!

We need to keep our core clean but we need AI agents to make our lives better.

The RICEFW That's Dying or May Die

Custom Reports: Joule agents can retrieve, analyze, and present data in natural language without ABAP.

Batch Interfaces: Agent-to-agent protocols mean your supplier's system can talk directly to your AR agent, which talks to your GL agent i.e. all governed, all audited, all in real-time.

Manual Conversions: AI-powered data migration agents can learn from your source system, apply business rules, and transform data without hand-coded conversion routines.

One-Off Enhancements: Process automation agents can handle exception scenarios, escalations, and edge cases without touching core code.

The Clean RICEFW That's Surviving (And Thriving)

Complex Business Logic Enhancements: Some customizations require deep process innovation that you want to control manually.

Industry-Specific Integrations: Niche vendor connections that are genuinely unique to your business.

Security/Compliance Modifications: Authorization logic and audit controls still need careful hand-crafting.

Legacy System Bridges: That complex old system nobody wants to talk about still needs complex interface that no one understands until they test it.

The RICEFW that survives is now optional by choice but with mandatory security and human in the loop verifications, not mandatory by technical limitation. You're choosing differentiating depth, not defaulting to it.

Can Your Business Actually Trigger This without violating security code of conduct?

This is where it gets hilarious and terrifying for the organizations at the same time.

In the old world, A business user could say: "Can we get a report showing customer profitability by region?" and I will then work out steps to increase the profitability.

Answer: No. Also, that'll be a 3-month custom development project, $100K, and a prayer to the NetWeaver gods.

In 2026 with Joule agents, A business user says: "I need to see which customers are bleeding money by region and automatically flag them for recovery.

Joule says: "Cool. I understand your GL, I know your customer master, I can apply your business rules, and I can trigger your AR team's dispute resolution agent when I find one. Also, I can set up real-time monitoring. Want me to trigger the pricing agent if a customer hits a threshold? I can do that too."

No development team needed. No governance nightmare yet. You need to validate and test the solution, whether it was developed by a human or an agent. Testing can also be automated, with human-in-the-loop verification to ensure quality and accuracy.

Terrifying and Exciting at the same time! But here's where it gets real.

The Business Enablement Problem (aka "Please Don't Break Everything")

The business can now trigger Joule. But the business also doesn't fully understand what "trigger" means in an agentic context. Because now you're not running a report. You're unleashing an autonomous decision-maker into your financial processes. Yes, business human-in-the-loop and agentic training represent the next trillion-dollar ERP opportunity.

Real Example Scenario from Q1 2026:

A business user asks Joule to automatically approve all invoices under $10K because "we trust our vendors".

Joule, being helpful, sets up an agent with broad approval authority.

Within 72 hours, a vendor with a typo in their master data starts sending $9,999.99 invoices and Finance doesn't notice because it's automating.

Suddenly your Q2 revenue recognition is off by $2.3M due to compliance issue.

This is not a hypothetical warning. It's already happening.

The Governance Reckoning - Why Your Old Org Chart Is Broken Now

Here's the uncomfortable truth. Your enterprise governance model was designed for humans. Humans are slow. Humans need approval workflows. Humans make mistakes, but predictable ones. Humans need audit trails because they're forgetful. Humans can't execute 10,000 transactions per second. Joule agents can do all of those things but need human in the loop verifications.

Unsupervised Agents can make bigger mistakes as they don't fear god or hell. They believe the logic they believe irrespective of whether it is right or wrong and don't listen until they are decommissioned or re-programmed.

Your current governance structure probably looks like this:

Business Analyst → Solution Architect → Technical Lead → Basis Team → Release Manager → Production.

The future governance structure may look like this if you don't change the Op Model explicitly and get your security policies right.

Business User →Solution Architect → Agent → Agent → Agent → Database → Reconciliation Nightmare → Technical and Basis Validation → Audit Finding.

No checkpoints. No control. Just speed and chaos if you don't fix your enterprise governance strategy and model.

The New Org Model for "Solution Design Authority"

In the agentic future, you need a fundamentally different operating model:

1. Agent Design Authority (New Role, Might Be You)

We don't need to automate every business requirement. Some things should stay as manual processes (yes, really). Your design authority decides which processes are "safe" for agent autonomy. How agents escalate to humans? Which business rules are non-negotiable?

Current state: Build me a report.

Agentic state: I'm going to autonomously make decisions affecting your cash position. Here are my constraints. Do you approve?

2. Data Governance Gets Paranoid (In a Good Way)

Agents are only as good as the data they touch. Your data governance team now owns the Data quality standards (agents will amplify bad data at light speed and Monthly or Weekly Master Data Cleansing won't work in agentic future).

Old question: How clean does our data need to be? Who are the business owners for each data object?

New question: How fast can our agents break if we don't fix this? Which objects agents can crash? Which agent owns the object and who is the business friend of the agent?

3. Authorization Models Get Microscopic

Remember when you had one "Finance Manager" role with broad approval authority? That was fine when one person held that role. Now that role might be inherited by 3 Joule agents, 2 citizen-built automations, and a third-party system via API.

Your Solution: Granular, agent-aware authorization design. Agents get micro-roles (not broad approval authority).Agent roles are time-bounded (expires after 90 days).

Agent actions are logged separately (so you can audit what "the AR agent" did vs. what "Sarah from AR" did).Segregation of duties needs to work across human AND agent actions.

4. Business Process Governance Becomes Real-Time

In the old model, you monitored exception reports on Friday. In the agentic model, you need real-time dashboards because agents can create 5 years worth of transactions in 3 hours.

New KPIs you actually need along with data quality and business process KPI's:

Agent decision distribution (is the pricing agent making reasonable decisions?)

Escalation rates (if agents are escalating 50% of cases, your rules are wrong)

Agent-vs-human performance (are agents faster, or just different-fast?)

Audit gap coverage (can you trace every decision to its source logic?)

The S/4 HANA Operational Model i.e. Five Things Your CTO Needs to Hear

1. Clean Data Is Not A Competitive Advantage anymore, It is Nutrition and Food for Agents

Companies with 95% master data quality will have agents that work. Companies with 75% quality will have agents that hallucinate, escalate constantly, and require human babysitting.

Budget allocation shift: Significant % of your S/4HANA investment should go to data quality, not fancy new reports.

2. Adopt Zero Tolerance Policy for Process Variations unless Agents can't bring Differentiating Value

Process standardization is not essential because SAP promotes a clean-core approach; however, it is essential for your business to remain thrive in an AI-driven world.

In the old world, you could have 47 different ways to process a PO because they all worked (kind of). With agents, you need ONE way. Or you need 47 agents configured identically. Pick your hell.

3. Human-Agent Collaboration Needs Explicit Designs

Agents aren't replacing humans. They're working alongside them. But you need to design this collaboration.

Where does the agent make autonomous decisions? Where does it pause and ask for human judgment? What does escalation actually mean? Can humans override agents? Should they?

The truth is 20% of agent's value comes from handling the routine. The remaining 80% comes from knowing when to stop and ask for help.

4. Testing Takes On New Meaning

You can't test an agent the way you test a form. Agents behave differently based on data, context, and rules you might not have explicitly configured.

Your QA needs:

Scenario-based and Boundary testing (not just the happy path, agent operating boundaries and exception processes if agent oversteps boundaries)

Adversarial and Security testing (what breaks this agent? who and what can stop this immortal agent?)

Data quality testing (will bad data cause unexpected behavior?)

Agent interaction testing (when two agents work together, do they amplify issues?)

Budget reality check: Plan for three times the testing effort required for traditional RICEFW customizations irrespective of whether your use or don't use test automation agents.

5. Change Management Needs to Happen in Weeks, Not Months

Here's the counterintuitive part. Because agents are less technical, business users will expect them to change faster. "Just tell Joule to do something different" sounds simple. But behind the scenes, you're changing business logic that affects financial records.

New change Management approach: Fast agent setup and business training. Continuous monitoring via dashboards. Quick rollback if issues arise. Ongoing updates to training and communications.

The below diagram is just an example.

Building Design Guardrails

Okay, serious time. Agentic AI in S/4HANA is powerful. Powerful things need guardrails. Here's what you actually need:

1. Decision Boundaries (The "No Absolutely Not" Layer)

Every agent needs explicit boundaries. Without boundaries, your agent becomes a decision-making black box. With them, you have an auditable, repeatable process.

Invoice Approval Agent Example: Can approve invoices under $10K. Cannot approve invoices from vendors flagged as "high risk". Cannot override compliance holds. Must escalate if invoice is >30 days old. Must escalate if vendor is new (< 90 days).

2. Explainability Requirements (The "Why?" Layer)

Your agent makes a decision. Your auditor asks: "Why?"

Agent says "I found a pattern in the data suggesting this customer is likely to churn, so I routed them to your VIP team. That's explainable". Joule agents log their reasoning. You need to build dashboards that surface this reasoning in real-time.

3. Escalation Pathways (The "Pause, Human" Layer)

An agent should escalate when it's at the boundary of its decision authority. It finds conflicting data. The situation is novel (it hasn't seen this before).There's regulatory sensitivity or It's just unsure.

Old exception model: Manual exception handling (humans notice problems after the fact)

New exception model: Agents escalate before problems happen. A human makes a judgment call. Decision gets logged and fed back to the agent as training. This creates a virtuous cycle and agents get smarter because humans are teaching them, in real-time.

4. Continuous Monitoring (The "Stay Awake" Layer)

You can't just deploy an agent and trust it. You need real-time dashboards showing Agent Approval Rates, Agent escalation times, Agent Error Rates, Human Override Rate etc.

The Practical Framework - RICEFW in the Agentic Age

Well we reached the end of RICEFW/FRICEW bedtime story. So if RICEFW doesn't die, what does it look like in 2026?

Reports will make over Reasoning Agents (AI-driven analysis and insights)

Interfaces will dress up as Agent Ecosystems (real-time agent-to-agent data exchange)

Conversions will disguise themselves as Continuous Transformations and Reconciliations Agents (real-time data intelligence)

Enhancements may change their wardrobe as Agentic Logic Workflows (autonomous process agents)

Forms will use Flow Intelligence to dynamically adapt their user experience and interface in real time to reflect each business profile, delivering a highly personalized experience with the same speed and flexibility that leading Hollywood actresses transform their appearance and role to suit a changing narrative.

Instead of annual change requests, you're doing sprint-based agent capability upgrades. Instead of 18-month implementations, you're doing 12-week agent activation waves.

RICEFW or FRICEW may be RAAFEA Agent 007 in future! Your SAP architect is no longer architecting enhancements. They're architecting how agents collaborate, how data flows between agents, and how everything stays governed.

entry.title: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Handling Missing Public APIs as a Partner — A Practical Guide
entry.content:
SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Handling Missing Public APIs as a Partner — A Practical Guide

Introduction

During SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition implementations and partner custom developments, partners occasionally encounter a scenario where a required API simply does not exist in the SAP Business Accelerator Hub. This gap can become a project blocker — particularly when third-party integrations or BTP side-by-side extensions depend on data objects that have no released API endpoint. During developer extensibiltiy on-stack customization of  SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition some of the required entities are not released for partner developement.

This blog post consolidates the recommended guidance for SAP partners on how to handle such situations. It covers the permanent resolution path via the SAP Customer Influence Programme (CIP), interim workaround options using Custom APIs, current known limitations, and the product improvements on SAP's roadmap.

Whether you are an implementation consultant, solution architect, partner enablement lead, or a partner developer, this guide provides the end-to-end picture.

The Scenario

You are mid-implementation of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition or in the process of building partner add-on of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Your solution requires an API — either to expose data to a BTP extension or to support an on-stack integration — and it is nowhere to be found on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

Before raising alarms, it is important to understand the two distinct types of APIs involved:

  • Local APIs — CDS views, Business Object Interfaces used in On-Stack Extensionsibility using ABAP Cloud
  • Remote APIs — APIs consumed externally, typically by BTP side-by-side applications or third-party systems.

This distinction determines both the CIP campaign you should target and the workaround approach you should implement in the interim.

Permanent Solution: The SAP Customer Influence Programme (CIP)

The right long-term path for any missing API on SAP Business Accelerator Hub is a formal request through the SAP Customer Influence Programme. Here is the recommended step-by-step process:

Note: SAP Continuos Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (CIP) would be moved to new Aha platform in near future and after the migration the CIP sessions and request URLs will be redirected to the Aha! platform after go-live.

Step 1 — Verify the API is Genuinely Missing

Before submitting any request, search SAP Business Accelerator Hub thoroughly. Confirm the API does not exist in any form — sometimes a different naming convention or an OData version difference can cause confusion.

Note: Please try out Joule copilot in SAP Business Accelerator Hub , It helps you with all your queries on the content available.

Note: make sure to select SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition in the product list in the SAP Business Accelerator Hub

Step 2 — Determine the API Type

Classify the missing API as either a Local API (on-stack) or a Remote API (external/BTP-facing). This classification determines which CIP campaign to use.

Step 3 — Check for an Existing CIP Request

Search the relevant campaign before creating a new entry. If another partner has already submitted the same request:

  • Vote for it. Every vote increases priority visibility with the SAP product team.

If no matching request exists, submit a new one. for more details please refer to SAP Community - Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition

Step 4 — Submit via the Correct CIP Campaign

 

API TypeCIP Campaign LinkNotes
Remote APIsCampaign 1175For APIs consumed by external apps or BTP side-by-side extensions (Loosely Couple Extensions using SAP BTP)
Local APIsCampaign 2759For on-stack APIs consumed within the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public system (Tightly Couple Extension using ABAP Cloud)

SLA Note: SAP targets a response within 20 business days of submission. For priority cases, partners can escalate via a partner support ticket / partner escallation channel.

For more detaila about CIP please refer to details below:

  • SAP Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - Frequently Asked Questions
  • SAP Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition - Session List and Rules of Engagement 
  • Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition | SAP Community

Temporary Workaround: Building a Custom API

While the CIP request works its way through the process, partners should not be left idle. Custom APIs provide a viable bridge. Two options are available as mentioned below.

Option 1: Custom CDS View Exposed as an External API

This is the preferred no-code/low-code approach that uses standard S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition on stack key user extensibility — no separate ABAP environment required.

Step 1 — Identify Released CDS Views Open the View Browser App in S/4HANA Cloud and locate released CDS views that can serve as the data source for your required API.

Step 2 — Create a Custom CDS View

  • Open the Custom CDS View App.
  • Select the relevant released CDS view(s) as the data source.
  • Add required fields, maintain field properties, and publish the Custom CDS View with the External API setting enabled.
  • Demo video - Creating Custom CDS Views as External APIs - SAP S/4HANA Cloud Extensibility

Step 3 — Expose via a Communication Scenario

  • Open the Custom Communication Scenario App and create a new Custom Communication Scenario.
  • Add the published Custom CDS View (External API) to the scenario and publish it.
  • Create a Communication Arrangement:
    • Assign the Custom Communication Scenario to the arrangement.
    • Create or maintain the Communication System and Communication User.
    • Activate the arrangement and copy the Service URL for testing.
  • Demo Video - Exposing Custom CDS Views as External APIs - SAP S/4HANA Cloud Extensibility

Step 4 — Test the Custom API Validate the endpoint using Postman or any API testing tool against the copied Service URL.

Note: The custom API's is a custom artifact created using above steps would allow Read-Only operation and would not support Create Update and Delete operations.

Option 2: RAP - Based API (ABAP Development)

For partners with access to an ABAP development environment — either BTP ABAP Environment or an S/4HANA Cloud development tenant — a RESTful ABAP Programming model (RAP) offers greater flexibility.

  1. Develop a RAP-based custom API using ABAP Development Tools (ADT).
  2. Release the custom API for ABAP Cloud consumption, making it a custom public API.
  3. Activate the released API via Communication Arrangements in the target tenant.

Custom API Delivery Approaches

Once a Custom API is built, partners need to decide how to deliver it — especially for multi-customer scenarios:

 

ApproachDescriptionBest Suited For
Multi Off (Multi-Customer Off-Stack)Package the custom API as part of an on-stack customization delivered via gCTS (Git-enabled Change and Transport System)Partners delivering solutions to few customers.
Scalable (Cross-Stack Extension)Combine an on-stack add-on (custom API on S/4HANA) with a side-by-side BTP extension that consumes the API.Packaged ABAP Cloud AddOn delivered  to customer via SAP Store using Landscape Portal.

Current Known Facts:

It would be remiss not to highlight the gaps that currently constrain these workarounds:

  1. Read-Only Operations Only: Custom APIs currently support only READ (GET) operations. Create, Update, and Delete (CUD) operations are not supported. This works as designed since CDS views are released for Readonly operation.

  2. Unreleased CDS Views: Not all CDS views have been released for custom use. This directly blocks Option 1 for certain data objects, forcing partners toward the more complex RAP-based approach or leaving them temporarily without a viable workaround. in such cases please follow CIP request approach.

  3. On-Stack Dependency for Multi-Tenant SaaS: Partners building multi-tenant SaaS applications that consume Custom APIs are required to deliver an on-stack extension component — adding architectural complexity and incremental cost to their delivery model. This works as designed since its a Cross Stack custom solution.

Summary and Recommended Actions

Here is a consolidated view of what partners should do today:

 

Area Recommended Action
CIP SubmissionCheck CIP campaigns 1175 (Remote) and 2759 (Local) — vote on existing requests or submit new ones.
Custom APIsUse Custom CDS Views (Option 1) or RAP wrappers (Option 2) as an interim workaround while CIP requests are processed.
CUD OperationsFlag any use cases requiring Create/Update/Delete operations — escalate via partner support if this is a project blocker.
CDS View GapsIf Option 1 is blocked due to an unreleased CDS view, submit via CIP Campaign 2759 and request fast-track review.
Multi-Tenant ArchitectureEngage with SAP Architecture / Partner Reference Applications (PRA) teams for guidance on on-stack add-on and cross-stack delivery models.

Closing Thoughts

Missing Public APIs need not be a dead-end for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition implementations. The path forward is clear: use the SAP Customer Influence Programme as the permanent vehicle for getting APIs officially released, and leverage Custom APIs as a structured, supported interim solution.

The combination of partner advocacy through CIP voting, tactical Custom API development, and SAP's roadmap commitments around CRUD support and CDS view releases should collectively close the gap — both today and over the coming release cycles.

If you have encountered similar challenges in your own S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition projects, consider voting on the relevant CIP campaigns and sharing your use case — your input directly shapes the product roadmap.

Key Reference Links

  • Overview | SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition | SAP Business Accelerator Hub
  • Remote APIs — CIP Campaign: https://influence.sap.com/sap/ino/#/campaign/1175
  • Local APIs — CIP Campaign : https://influence.sap.com/sap/ino/#/campaign/2759
  • SAP Community Blog Post - New Guided Missions for SAP Partners: Build Once. Scale to Many
  • Build Solutions for SAP Cloud ERP with confidence - SAP Community

This blog post is based on guidance current as of 2026. The CRUD operation gap and unreleased CDS view limitations are actively tracked as product improvement items.

entry.title: SAP Integration Suite MCP in Action: Integrating SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox with AI Client
entry.content:
Introduction

This article builds upon the excellent foundational blog by Ashutosh Singh, "MCP Servers on SAP Integration Suite: Build Your First MCP Server from an API Artifact" - MCP Servers on SAP Integration Suite : Build Your ... - SAP Community. Readers looking for detailed guidance on the initial MCP setup should first refer to that article, which covers:

  • SAP Integration Suite prerequisites and role assignments
  • Integration Cell Runtime setup
  • API Artifact creation
  • MCP Artifact creation
  • MCP deployment and activation

The objective of this blog is not to repeat those foundational steps. Instead, it focuses on extending the MCP scenario by integrating SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition Sandbox APIs with SAP Integration Suite MCP Server and consuming the exposed MCP capabilities using Cline in Visual Studio Code.

Note: - While this article demonstrates the solution using Cline, the same MCP server can be consumed by other MCP-compatible AI clients such as Claude Desktop/Code, Github Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, or organizational AI assistants. This flexibility allows organizations to standardize on SAP Integration Suite as the MCP provider while allowing freedom in AI client selection.

Specifically, this article demonstrates how to:

  • Configure connectivity from SAP Integration Suite to the SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox environment
  • Configure destination and API access using SAP Business Accelerator Hub API keys
  • Expose SAP Business Partner APIs through an MCP Artifact
  • Get OAuth Token using Postman
  • Configure and connect Cline as an MCP client in Visual Studio Code
  • Query SAP business data using natural language and receive AI-generated business summaries

Although some topics such as Destinations, API Artifacts, and MCP Artifacts are briefly revisited, the focus here is on their configuration for SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox connectivity, which differs from the generic setup covered in the reference article.

Why This Scenario?

The SAP Business Accelerator Hub Sandbox provides a simple and cost-effective way to experiment with SAP APIs without requiring access to a productive SAP S/4HANA Cloud tenant.

By combining:

  • SAP Integration Suite MCP Server
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub Sandbox APIs
  • Cline as an MCP-compatible AI client

developers can quickly build conversational AI experiences that transform SAP business data into natural language insights.

 

Solution Architecture

The solution uses SAP Integration Suite as the bridge between an AI client and SAP business data exposed through SAP Business Accelerator Hub Sandbox APIs.

Reference architecture for SAP Integration Suite MCP and SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox.

Step 1 – User Interaction through Cline

A user submits a natural language query in Visual Studio Code using Cline.

Example: Summarize Business Partner 11

Step 2 – SAP Integration Suite MCP Artifact

The MCP Artifact exposes SAP Business Partner APIs as MCP tools that can be discovered and invoked by MCP-compatible AI clients.

The MCP Artifact publishes:

  • Tools
  • Resources
  • Prompts

Step 3 – SAP Integration Suite API Artifact

The MCP tool invokes an API Artifact responsible for connectivity, mediation, and API management.

This allows organizations to reuse Integration Suite capabilities such as:

  • Security
  • Connectivity
  • Monitoring
  • Governance

Step 4 – SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox

The API Artifact invokes the Business Partner API available through SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

In this implementation:

API_BUSINESS_PARTNER

is used as the backend service.

Step 5 – AI Generated Business Summary

The Business Partner data is returned through MCP, and the AI client generates a natural language response.

Example:

Business Partner 11 is registered under the name Cust15 Cust15. The record belongs to category 2 and was created on 25 May 2018. No customer or supplier role is currently assigned.

Step 1 – Configure Destination in SAP Integration Suite

The first step is to establish connectivity between SAP Integration Suite and the SAP Business Accelerator Hub Sandbox.

Configure a destination using:

Create a destination (subaccount -> Destinations-> Create) pointing to https://sandbox.api.sap.com

Destination configuration for SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox

Authentication is performed through API Key obtained from SAP Business Accelerator Hub which can be seen in step 2 of this blog.

Step 2 – Create API Artifact in SAP Integration Suite

Create an API Artifact for API_BUSINESS_PARTNER. Use optimized query parameters such as $top and $select to reduce payload size.

Select destination created in Step 1.

Select Destination under API Provider

Business Partner API Resources View

 Login URL: https://api.sap.com/api/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/overview

S4HANA Public Cloud Business Partner API Key

Define Authentication Type

Define Scope for Authorization

Content Modifier Configuration under Policies

Configuration of Business Partner API in HTTP Receiver adapter

Address:

https://sandbox.api.sap.com/s4hanacloud/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER

For faster execution, I have optimized the query as below for testing purpose:

$top=10&$select=BusinessPartner,BusinessPartnerName,BusinessPartnerCategory,BusinessPartnerGrouping,Customer,Supplier,CreatedByUser,CreationDate

Step 3 – Create MCP Artifact in SAP Integration Suite

Create an MCP Artifact and associate it with the API Artifact. 

Select API Artifact created in Step 2

Add tools from exposed Business Partner API.

Example tools generated in this scenario:

  • get_A_BusinessPartner
  • get_A_BusinessPartner_BusinessPartner
  • post_A_BusinessPartner (We are not executing this as part of this blog, only for showing how to add multiple methods as tools)

Arguments Configuration in Prompts

Once deployed, the MCP Artifact automatically exposes operations as MCP tools, resources and prompts as defined.

Policy view of MCP Artifact

MCP URL shown above will be used in Postman and Cline to expose MCP operations.

Note: Any changes to policies can be synchronized based on API Artifact change but it can’t be edited directly in MCP artifact except HTTP receiver adapter details like timeout and header details.

Step 4 – OAuth Token Retrieval Using Postman

OAuth Token Retrieval

Retrieve an OAuth access token for the MCP endpoint.

HTTP Request for Token Generation

Client ID, Client Secret and OAuth Token URL can be obtained from SAP BTP using path: Subaccount -> Instances and Subscriptions -> Instance -> Service Keys – View

SAP Integration Suite Credential View

Get Generated OAuth Token

Copy Generated Token

Optionally, you can also view MCP tools, resources and prompts in Postman by passing Bearer token generated previously to SAP 

Successful MCP Tool Prompts Resources Invocation

Step 5 – Install and Configure Cline in Visual Studio Code

To consume the MCP server from an AI client, install the Cline extension from the Visual Studio Code Marketplace.

Installing the Cline extension from Visual Studio Code Marketplace

After installation, configure a Remote MCP Server.

Edit Cline MCP Settings in JSON

Cline MCP settings JSON file and save using Ctrl+S

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "SAP-BusinessPartner": {
      "url": "https:// <mcp-endpoint from SAP Integration Suite>",
      "type": "streamableHttp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer {{token generated in Step 4 of Postman}}"
      },
      "autoApprove": []
    }
  }
}

Updated Cline MCP server configuration

Step 6 – Verify MCP Discovery

After connecting successfully, Cline should discover the capabilities exposed through the MCP Artifact.

Successful discovery of MCP capabilities in Cline.

At this point, the SAP Integration Suite MCP Server is fully consumable through the AI client.

 

Connectivity Tip: If Cline cannot connect to the MCP server, errors such as Fetch failed, connection timeout, 401/403 authorization errors, or tool discovery failures may indicate corporate firewall, proxy, or VPN restrictions. Verify endpoint accessibility, proxy configuration, and OAuth connectivity before troubleshooting the MCP configuration itself.

 

Natural Language Interaction

One of the most interesting aspects of MCP is that business users can interact with SAP data using natural language rather than API calls.

Example Prompt

Use the Business Partner tool and provide a concise executive summary of the retrieved business partner record. Include the business partner name, category, creation date, and whether customer or supplier roles are assigned. Avoid technical SAP terminology.

Response

Response in Cline based on Request to SAP Integration Suite MCP URL

Note: This business summary was generated using Cline as the AI client. Depending on the AI client, model, prompt configuration, and response settings, the generated text may differ. However, the underlying SAP Business Partner information retrieved through the SAP Integration Suite MCP tool remains unchanged.

 

Lessons Learned

MCP Tools Work Seamlessly

Business Partner APIs exposed through SAP Integration Suite MCP were automatically discoverable and consumable through Cline.

Payload Optimization Matters

Limiting the API response using $select produced cleaner AI-generated summaries and reduced response times.

 

Conclusion

SAP Integration Suite MCP Server provides a powerful mechanism for exposing SAP business capabilities to AI clients.

By combining:

  • SAP Integration Suite
  • MCP Artifacts
  • SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud Sandbox APIs
  • AI client

it becomes possible to transform traditional SAP APIs into conversational business capabilities.

This approach offers a practical starting point for organizations looking to explore MCP, AI-assisted development, and natural language access to SAP business data.

Thank you for reading. I hope this blog helps you kick-start your SAP Integration Suite MCP journey with SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud APIs. If you have any questions, suggestions, or ideas for extending this scenario, please feel free to leave a comment below.
